title: What the mix means in rupees
objectives: Translate three mixes into rupee outcomes.
Explain the trade-off between the expected result and the falls on the way.
body_md:
Clients agree with percentages and decide with rupees. Show both.

## ₹10 lakh for 15 years

Assuming equity 12%, debt 7%, gold 8% and a fixed deposit 6.5% a year, rebalanced yearly, before tax:

| Mix | Blended return | Value at year 15 |
|---|---|---|
| 100% fixed deposit (6.5%) | 6.5% | ≈ ₹25.7 L |
| Conservative 30/60/10 | ≈ 8.6% | ≈ ₹34.5 L |
| Moderate 50/40/10 | ≈ 9.6% | ≈ ₹39.6 L |
| Aggressive 70/20/10 | ≈ 10.6% | ≈ ₹45.3 L |

## Read the table honestly

More equity means a higher expected result and bigger falls on the way. The aggressive row is not automatically the right answer: the right row is the one the client can stay with through a bad year.

## Label it

Every figure here is illustrative, with stated assumptions, before tax. Never present it as a forecast or a promise.
example: A 52-year-old with ₹30 lakh in fixed deposits sees that the FD row reaches about ₹25.7 lakh in 15 years while a conservative mix reaches about ₹34.5 lakh at assumed returns. The illustration opens the conversation; the risk profile decides it.
say: At the assumptions shown, the conservative mix reaches about ₹34.5 lakh against about ₹25.7 lakh in fixed deposits.
The right row is the one you can stay with through a bad year, not the highest one.
never: This mix will give you ₹45 lakh.
The aggressive mix is the best choice for everyone.

check.q: In the ₹10 L, 15-year illustration, the moderate mix reached about…
check.why: About ₹39.6 L at the assumed returns; not a forecast.

check.q: Which row reached about ₹25.7 lakh in the illustration?
check.why: A fixed deposit at 6.5% reaches about ₹25.7 L, less than the conservative mix at assumed returns.

check.q: What must accompany every projection like this?
o: The label 'illustrative', the assumptions and the fact that it is before tax
A comparison with a bank FD
check.why: Label it illustrative, state the assumptions and say it is before tax. Never present it as a promise.
